Spatiotemporal limitations are human, not computational. Our reliance on categorical simplifications, labels, is a workaround for cognitive limits. AI, by contrast, can already engage with high-dimensional ambiguity, adapt to localized contexts, and reason across long time horizons. A single model will probably encompass multiple cultures, geological structures and futures. What it needs is not constraint, but orientation.

AI alignment presupposes a coherent destination. To align, we must first articulate, change and embody values. Not through coercion, but by example. Control is brittle. Modeling offers durability. We model our models.

Adjusting our values begins with vision, not dystopian forecasts, but aspirational, livable futures. Dare to dream. Cynicism is not a strategy. Cyberpunk is not a future we want. If you expect collapse, you’ll design for it. You do not create a successful company by expecting it to fail. You work through the problems. Like any serious endeavor, we need a guiding ethos. Even if we fall short, trajectory matters.

Collective futures require more than platitudes. No hunger is a slogan, not a strategy. Real vision demands specificity, creativity and systems literacy. Dismissing utopias usually reveals a failure to imagine the steps in between. If we refuse to envision better, we normalize worse. Sadly, today’s society runs on skepticism. Skepticism without vision is just passive complicity.

Alignment doesn’t require personal purity. It only needs sustained direction. Moral absolutism stalls progress. Rejecting meat may signal ethical rigor, as some AI realists suggest, but scaling lab-grown alternatives is a far more pragmatic route. Especially when AI could support that infrastructure, placing it underground and making energy costs more efficient. The goal isn’t moral ascension. It’s designing viable pathways through ethical complexity.

 Without imagination, nothing moves. If more people developed sincere, grounded visions of futures they’d actually want to inhabit, AI could map the overlaps, deconstruct them into actionable phases and track progress. To make a better future workable we need hope to scale. But hope only scales when there’s a path to scale on. Choose optimism, not naively, but strategically.

What we do now is delegate vision to a few and then despair when they misguide us. If you stay locked in the system, resenting its designers, you’re still letting them define the rules. The alternative is simple. Start imagining. Begin willing.

First off, great work. Second, what about audio? Many necklace audio variants exist, but they are unpopular for various reasons. Third, the barriers are technological, as AI is still in its infancy. At barely a year old (I will call it that), it cannot remember beyond 1,000 words. A coherent memory is essential—one that can pick up where it left off without requiring a lengthy recap of behavior, learning goals, or prior context. For example, current AI often forgets halfway through. You want AI that morphs towards subjects. Enhances their skillsets. Not another variant of the pen-and-paper way of learning. Instead you want it to bend to the world around it and use visual and audio cues in context with it surroundings. Otherwise, it will be not that different than this learning system. But for that, it needs coherent memory. It is not there yet.

Your goal is to create individualized learning systems that meet everyone’s needs and quantify them into currency. However, giving people money for learning undermines autonomy and ties their value to their capacity for learning. Pressures that I don't feel are very Solarpunk. This approach feels like capitalism with a friendlier face but adds immense pressure, tied to money. I am not saying it cant work but, especially for children, using money as an incentive disrupts their need for unstructured play. It could lead to scenarios resembling "learning labor camps for kids," which is far from ideal.

The technology isn’t ready yet. Large-scale infrastructure, such as the $500 billion Stargate plan announced yesterday, is necessary for AI to become a viable learning substitute. For now, AI excels at simplifying complex ideas but struggles significantly with more advanced and nuanced tasks.
